evidence_notes: Claim: driverless cars should not exist, humans should keep control. Support is hypothetical/assertive (route can't be changed mid-trip; computer could glitch; laziness; as expensive as hiring a driver) with no named case or figure. org 4 (thesis first sentence, opening+closing present, both body parts relate; rung 5 NO - the control paragraph and the laziness/expense paragraph swap freely; para 3 also carries several jobs without returning). dev 3 (rung 3 YES on the one realized scenario of wanting to change route, but support is otherwise general and the 'explanations' are near-circular restatements - dangerous because not safe; several claims, e.g. cost equivalence, unsupported). conv 3 (rung 3 YES - meaning always recoverable; rung 4 NO - 'Although be driven by a computer... but it's not' and the comma-spliced 'very dangerous, it is not safe to not be driven by someone with a right mind' force repair re-reads; controll/andymore/rode accumulate). arg 4 (rung 4 YES on the route-flexibility reason, which states why loss of control matters; rung 5 NO - the 'may seem safe and trustworthy' concession is denied, not answered, no principle made explicit, conclusion is what the for/against framing implies).

Claim: you should volunteer as a seagoing cowboy; five listed advantages (character, helping people, free sightseeing, avoiding the draft, fun on the return trip), source material recast into first-person anecdote (Acropolis, gondola ride, ping-pong/fencing tournaments, turning 18 aboard). org 4 (thesis in opening, hook and summative closing present, every part is an advantage; rung 5 NO - the five advantage paragraphs are a freely reorderable list). dev 4 (rung 3 YES - Acropolis, gondola, named games; rung 4 YES - 'you get to see these things for free because you have to go to some places', 'nothing to do so to pass the time'; rung 5 NO - the character and helping-people paragraphs are general and circular, so support is not specific throughout). conv 3 (rung 3 YES; rung 4 NO - 'you have to do work all the time so you are busy so then if you have to you can learn how to clean...' needs repair, and the draft paragraph requires a re-read; Iturned/grondola/volleball/afun/cowbot accumulate). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - the free-sightseeing reason states why it follows from the job itself; rung 5 NO - no opposing view, no qualification, no explicit governing principle).

Claim: driverless cars would be an influential addition to transportation, but should only be allowed once fully tested and safe. Two block quotations from the source (Brin's driverless taxi fleet using half the fuel; illegality of testing plus the liability-law gap), each followed by a one-sentence gloss. org 4 (thesis stated early and held, conclusion present; rung 5 NO - the benefit paragraph and the testing paragraph could swap with little loss and the closing only restates the opening's two clauses). dev 4 (rung 3 YES - quoted particulars; rung 4 YES - 'This would be usefull to people around the globe who don,t have cars' and 'This Exert from the passage supports my claim...'; rung 5 NO - glosses restate rather than add, and the traffic-ease claim goes unsupported; quotations are marked but sit alongside rather than inside the writer's sentences). conv 3 (rung 3 YES; rung 4 NO - the unpunctuated opening sentence must be re-segmented, and errors accumulate: aloud for allowed four times, influeintial, sociaty, pat, don,t, Exert). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - explains why the fleet matters, it serves people who cannot afford cars; rung 5 NO - the safety qualification is taken over from the source and the verdict stays inside the prompt's for/against framing, with the second body reason asserted rather than reasoned).

Claim: emotion-reading technology would be valuable in the classroom. Two source quotations (the smile/frown web-ad line; the computer recognizing a confused or bored student), the second genuinely unpacked - the teacher is busy with one student while others struggle, so the computer adapts the question. org 4 (controlling idea in the first sentence and held, opening and closing both present, both supports relate; rung 5 NO - the sad-student and confused-student sections are interchangeable). dev 4 (rung 3 YES - quoted particulars; rung 4 YES - 'This means if the main teachor is telling someone else...'; rung 5 NO - the web-ad quote barely bears on the sadness claim and its gloss only restates, so explanation is inconsistent and several claims - 'so many advantages' - go unsupported). conv 3 (rung 3 YES; rung 4 NO - the run-on 'then the computer could help them and see their their emotion and it would change the question' and the spliced 'not understand the question, well this technology could help that' need repair; vaulable/woud/diffirence/thier/teachor accumulate). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - states why the tech helps: a teacher's attention is limited and the computer detects what the teacher misses; rung 5 NO - no opposing consideration, no qualification, no explicit principle, and the conclusion is what the prompt implies).

Claim: development of driverless cars should cease. Three reasons - they breed laziness, drivers will use the car as a scapegoat despite the law making the driver responsible, and malfunction raises accident and death rates. The liability law is the one concrete piece of borrowed fact and is put to work. org 4 (thesis at the end of the intro and held, opening and closing do their jobs, all three parts relate; rung 5 NO - the three objections are independent and reorderable, the link back to laziness being a cohesive tag rather than a dependency). dev 4 (rung 3 YES - the driver-responsibility law; rung 4 YES - explains that the driver will invoke the car to dodge court cases; rung 5 NO - laziness and malfunction are general speculation with restatement-level explanation, so support is not specific throughout). conv 4 (rung 4 YES - errors are few and nothing needs repair; rung 5 NO - 'work almost efficiently', 'raise the intelligence of some drivers' and 'a new thing' wrong-foot the reader, and many sentences repeat one this-is/it-can shape). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - the scapegoat reason states why it follows from the existing liability rule; rung 5 NO - the three concessions are denied by asserting malfunction risk rather than answered, and the verdict stays inside the prompt's framing).

Claim: against driverless cars, prefers to drive manually. Reasons: taxis already exist, driving is enjoyable and free, drivers/chauffeurs lose their livelihoods, and malfunction or hacking creates danger and legal blame. org 4 (thesis in the first sentence with a preview, closing recaps, every part relates to opposing driverless cars; rung 5 NO - jobs, enjoyment and danger are interchangeable, and the preview order does not match the body order). dev 4 (rung 3 YES - the displaced bus/taxi/chauffeur drivers who did not attend college, and the hacker who drives you out of state; rung 4 YES - defect leads to accident leads to blame leads to fines or jail is a stated chain; rung 5 NO - 'I enjoy driving' is bare assertion and much else is unsupported). conv 2 (rung 2 YES; rung 3 NO - 'But what if your just like antother day of you letting your car drive itself starts to have defects' and 'it may read that its a possibility of that' require guessing at intent, not just repair; frequent fragments and non-resolving sentences alongside dozens of spelling slips). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - the jobs reason says why: no college, no alternative work; the freedom reason says why: go where and when you want; rung 5 NO - 'self driving cars would be nice to have' is mere mention, no qualification or explicit principle, conclusion implied by the framing).

Position: the Seagoing Cowboys program is a good program worth signing up for - but the first half is source summary (hay and oats for 335 horses; Luke Bomberger saying it made him aware of other countries' needs) and the persuasive claim only emerges in the last two paragraphs. org 3 (rung 3 YES - a controlling idea is stated; rung 4 NO - it is weakly located, arriving late, since the opening merely describes what the program does rather than stating the position it will hold). dev 3 (rung 3 YES - the 335-horses figure and the named Bomberger testimony; rung 4 NO - the figure and the testimony are reported and then followed by unconnected assertions of life-change, so the reader supplies the link; the Bomberger material is attributed but barely transformed). conv 2 (rung 2 YES; rung 3 NO - 'Once they cared cows and mules from overseas' cannot be repaired without guessing whether they carried or cared for them, and the fragment 'To help others with there problems' leaves its job to be guessed; suspective, 'You also be more grateful', 'could really could', there/their throughout). arg 3 (rung 3 YES - the position is committed by the close; rung 4 NO - the closing paragraphs circle, restating 'it could change your life' in new words, and the one because-clause justifies a restated benefit rather than showing why the position follows).

Written in persona as Luke Bomberger. Position: being a Seagoing Cowboy was an opportunity of a lifetime - it delivered aid to countries ruined by the war and opened up the world. Support is dense and specific: animals and feed to bombed-out countries, ball games in the emptied stalls, the Acropolis, a Venice gondola, an excavated Cretan castle, the Panama Canal. org 4 (opening states the dual controlling idea and holds it, closing adds the draft point rather than restating; rung 5 NO - the recreation and sightseeing paragraphs are interchangeable). dev 4 (rung 3 YES; rung 4 YES - 'Helping them helped me to be more aware of people of other countries and their needs' and the closing tie the experiences to the claim; rung 5 NO - the games and the monuments are catalogued without individual interpretive work, so explanation is not applied to most of the support). conv 4 (rung 4 YES - errors are minimal, sentences vary in length and shape, the 'See the Acropolis' fragment is controlled; rung 5 NO - 'So many people, that would have otherwise not have been able to do very well, got animals...' loses its grip and costs a re-read). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - states why the program mattered: it reached people who would otherwise not have managed, and that changed the narrator's awareness; rung 5 NO - no opposing consideration, no qualification of the position, no explicit governing principle).

Claim: the Face on Mars is a natural landform, not an alien monument. Support drawn from the source: the sharper second photograph, the pixel rule of thumb quote, and the Middle Butte in the Snake River of Idaho comparison. org 4 (claim in the first sentence and held, opening and closing present, every part bears on it; rung 5 NO - the general landform paragraph and the photographic-evidence paragraph swap freely, the winter/location aside wanders, and the closing repeats the second paragraph). dev 3 (rung 3 YES and rung 4 nominally met by 'This tell us that...' - but 'It also tell us that it actually shows is the Martian equivalent of a butte or a mesa, which is landforms that are normal around the American West' is unmarked source phrasing lightly stitched in, i.e. patchwriting, which caps the trait at 3; the pixel-rule gloss also misfires and the opening assertions are unsupported). conv 3 (rung 3 YES - meaning stays recoverable; rung 4 NO - 'Some people think that just because it is a face that was created by Aliens because it looks to much like a face' and the garbled 'it actually shows is' both need repair; could of, This tell us, coincedence, 'look like ours and is like ours' accumulate). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - argues that because natural landforms come in all shapes, a face-shaped one needs no alien explanation, and that the enlarged image showed a mesa; rung 5 NO - the closing does answer the alien inference, but the conclusion is exactly the one the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: emotion-reading technology should not be used on students. Reasons: expressions do not reliably reveal feeling (people stay angry while acting fine; a fake smile is not happiness), so FACS reads only what it infers from the face; and the source's own paragraph 9 concedes only that smile muscles make you slightly happy. org 4 (position in the first sentence and held, opening orients and 'Therefore, to end my argument' closes, both reasons relate; rung 5 NO - the emotional-harm opening and the unreliability paragraph could swap without loss). dev 4 (rung 3 YES - the cited paragraph 9 claim and the observed masking behaviour; rung 4 YES - 'This means it can make you SLIGHTLY happy but not enough to classify yourself as happy' and the FACS-infers-rather-than-reads line both state the connection and add to it; rung 5 NO - the opening claim that students get sadder is bare assertion, so support is not specific throughout). conv 4 (rung 4 YES - errors are few and nothing needs repair; rung 5 NO - 'approve to let', 'forsure' and 'that is when it gets weird' wrong-foot the reader and sentence shapes are limited). arg 4 (rung 4 YES - genuinely reasons that expression and feeling are dissociable, so the system reads inference not emotion; rung 5 NO - it answers a minor source point rather than the strongest pro case, and the conclusion goes no further than its own supporting reasons).
